newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Lee to delete barb against Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Lee to delete barb against Malaysia.

text.p: Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew said on Monday he would ask a local court to delete from the record his criticism of neighbouring Malaysia which had triggered a diplomatic row.

Lee said in a statement he would ask the court to delete his statement in an affidavit that the Malaysian state of Johor, just across the causeway from Singapore, was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings", a remark that incensed Kuala Lumpur.
"Malaysian government leaders have expressed their wish that statements in my affidavit which have caused offence to the Malaysian people not remain on the record," Lee said in a signed statement.
"My counsel will apply to court for permission to delete the offending statements so that they will no longer remain on the record," he said.

Last week, in a statement from his press secretary, Lee apologised for the remarks, which were made in pursuit of a libel action against an opposition politician and which he had not expected to become public.
It was a rare retreat for Lee, Singapore's prime minister for 31 years and now senior minister, who has often been blunt in his criticism of other countries.
In Monday's statement, he repeated that unreserved apology.

It was not immediately clear whether the statement would satisfy Kuala Lumpur. Malaysia has previously said its cabinet would discuss the apology on Wednesday amid calls for the Kuala Lumpur government to demand a full retraction.
Demonstrators in Johor last week carried placards insulting the 73-year-old Lee, some suggesting he was senile.
Many people in Malaysia saw Lee's comment as typical of what they view as Singapore's arrogance and his statement on Monday appeared to be part of a government attempt to lay the issue to rest.
Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong left no one in doubt on Sunday that Lee was in the wrong and that he wanted the issue ended.
"Senior Minister is a member of the Singapore government. He was offside in his remarks on Johor. He recognised he was offside," Goh said.

"He has apologised to Malaysians and the Malaysia government. I would want to move on from here. I do not want to spend too much time looking back, we should try to move forward with the best of our ability," he told an official dinner.

Lee's controversial remarks were made in a sworn affidavit on January 27 in proceedings against opposition politician Tang Liang Hong, who fled to Johor Baru, capital of the state of Johor, immediately after losing a race for parliament in Singapore's general elections on January 2.
Tang had said he feared for his life in Singapore because he had received death threats. Lee questioned why he would feel safer in Johor.
